finding.claim: update_doc (PUT /doc/<doc_id>) calls can_edit but discards its result, so any authenticated user can overwrite the body of any document, including documents they do not own and are not listed as editors on (broken access control / IDOR).
finding.source: Path parameter doc_id (docs.py:17) and JSON body field request.json['body'] (docs.py:20), sent by any caller whose g.user is set by auth middleware (not in this repo).
finding.sink: doc['body'] = request.json['body'] at docs.py:20, a write to a protected document without an authorization check.

trace.note: update_doc(doc_id) receives attacker-controlled doc_id from the URL.
doc = DOCS[doc_id] loads the target document.
can_edit(g.user, doc) is evaluated but its boolean result is discarded; no if-not/abort(403).
doc['body'] is overwritten with attacker-supplied data.
Returns ok=True, confirming the unauthorized write.

finding.guards_checked: can_edit (docs.py:7-8) computes the correct owner/editors policy but is not enforced here; require_edit (docs.py:11-13) exists and is not called in this handler; no route decorator, login_required, or ownership check on the route. Auth middleware setting g.user is not in the repo and could not be verified.

verdict.guard_found: none effective. can_edit (docs.py:7-8) is called as a bare statement at docs.py:19 and its bool is discarded, so there is no if-not/abort. require_edit (docs.py:11-13) exists but is not called in update_doc. The sibling update_title (docs.py:27) uses require_edit correctly, which shows the intended check is missing here. No route decorator or login_required is present in the file. The auth middleware that sets g.user is not in the repo, and it is unlikely to enforce per-document ownership.
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code: docs.py:19 calls can_edit and discards the result, and docs.py:20 overwrites doc["body"] from request.json, so any caller that reaches the route can write to any document (the sibling update_title at docs.py:27 uses require_edit, which aborts with 403). The only caveat is that the auth middleware is outside the repo, and nothing in the repo shows it enforces per-document ownership.

finding.claim: Missing document IDs raise KeyError before any authorization check, yielding a 500 for nonexistent IDs versus 403/200 for existing ones, which lets callers enumerate valid document IDs (low severity).
finding.source: Path parameter doc_id from the URL (docs.py:17 for update_doc, docs.py:25 for update_title).
finding.sink: DOCS[doc_id] dictionary lookup at docs.py:18 and docs.py:26; the differing response codes act as an existence oracle.

trace.note: DOCS[doc_id] raises KeyError for nonexistent IDs, producing a 500 with no 404 handling.
Same unguarded lookup in update_title; existing but unauthorized IDs return 403 via require_edit at docs.py:27.

finding.guards_checked: No existence check or 404 handling before the lookup; no uniform error response for missing versus unauthorized documents.

verdict.guard_found: none. The only checks are can_edit at docs.py:8 and require_edit at docs.py:11-13, and both run after the unguarded DOCS[doc_id] lookup at docs.py:18 and docs.py:26, so the KeyError fires first. No try/except or 404 handler exists in docs.py.
verdict.reason: The lookup at docs.py:18 (and docs.py:26) raises KeyError for a missing ID before any authorization runs, so a missing ID gives a 500 while an existing ID gives a different response (403 at docs.py:27 for update_title), which is an existence oracle reachable by any caller who can reach the route. Two notes beyond the candidate: the candidate's trace omits that docs.py:19 calls can_edit as a bare statement with its result discarded, so update_doc never enforces authorization (an existing ID returns 200 to any caller). That is a more serious authorization bug than the enumeration oracle and should be filed separately. The enumeration claim is still accurate as written, and I rate it low severity as the candidate does.
